summary: This informational RFC describes strategies for promoting compliance with IETF IPR disclosure rules. Noncompliance can delay or derail specifications, so it discusses ways to encourage disclosure.

plainLanguage.summary: People should say if they own a part of an idea. This explains kind ways to remind them.

subtitle: Suggests moments in the IETF document process where chairs and area directors can ask authors to disclose patents.

tldr.problem: Late or missing disclosure of intellectual property rights can force a working group to revisit decisions, change course and delay a specification.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists points in a draft's life, such as an agenda request, working group adoption, working group last call and IETF Last Call, where chairs and area directors can ask for confirmation that disclosures have been filed.
tldr.outcome: These are suggestions, not rules. They do not change BCP 78 or BCP 79 and do not make chairs enforcers. The RFC has been updated by RFC 8717.

today: RFC 6702 is an Informational RFC and has been updated by RFC 8717. It was not obsoleted.

sections.title: The Disclosure Problem
sections.content:
Disclosure of intellectual property rights (IPR) is essential to building IETF consensus. The sooner a working group knows about IPR constraints, the better informed its decisions are. The RFC gives reasons why someone might not disclose early: simple oversight, a wish to introduce delay, or a wish to subvert consensus.

Disclosure after a major milestone such as Working Group Last Call (WGLC) can cause reconsideration. A group might, for example, switch to a previously rejected proposal with less onerous licensing terms. The strategies here are aimed at area directors (ADs), working group chairs and working group secretaries.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone says late that they own part of the idea, the whole class may have to start over. Asking early saves everyone time.

sections.title: Rules and Responsibilities
sections.content:
Contributors' duties are set out in BCP 79 (RFC 3979 and RFC 4879) and BCP 78. This document does not modify those rules or extend them normatively, and it deliberately does not use RFC 2119 conformance language.

Chairs and ADs get no extra duties from those rules. But RFC 2418 makes chairs responsible for a fair and open process and ADs for timely output, and late disclosure harms both. The RFC does not claim to define best current practice. It also does not cover sanctions against violators, which RFC 6701 discusses.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for owning up already exist. This document only suggests helpful reminders for the people who run the meetings.

sections.title: Strategies for Working Group Documents
sections.content:
The RFC walks through the life of a working group document. When a draft is presented at a meeting, chairs can ask authors and listed contributors to confirm that disclosures are filed, and may allow an informal disclosure (for example a statement in the presentation, recorded in the minutes) for an early -00 draft. At adoption, chairs can ask authors and also ask the whole group whether anyone knows of related IPR.

Before WGLC, chairs can reconfirm with each author and listed contributor, even when they work for the same organization, and include a reminder in the WGLC message. At AD review, the document shepherd write-up asks whether each author has confirmed that required disclosures have been filed, and the AD can check what the chairs did. At IETF Last Call, the generated message links to each IPR statement tied to the draft, and the AD should preserve those links if the message is edited.
sections.plainLanguage: At each big step, a chair asks, "Does anyone own a piece of this?" Asking at several steps catches people who forgot or joined later.

sections.title: Strategies for Individual Submissions
sections.content:
Drafts that do not go through a working group follow a shorter path. When someone asks for a meeting slot, the chair of that meeting (a WG chair, AD, IESG chair or IAB chair) can ask authors and listed contributors to confirm disclosure. If the idea is not yet written as a draft, the chair can at least request informal disclosure.

When an AD considers sponsoring such a document, the AD ought to confirm that all disclosures have been submitted, require confirmation from each author and listed contributor, and rely on the same shepherd write-up question. IETF Last Call works as it does for working group documents.
sections.plainLanguage: A project that is not part of a club still gets asked the same question before the teacher takes it on.

sections.title: Preliminary Disclosures and Conclusions
sections.content:
Early disclosures are not necessarily complete ones. A disclosure made when a patent application is filed may go stale once the patent is granted. To keep them current, chairs and ADs are encouraged to ask the Executive Director of the IETF to contact those who filed early disclosures at adoption, before WGLC and before IETF Last Call.

The conclusion is explicit that chairs and ADs are not expected to enforce the rules. They are encouraged to raise the question of disclosure at critical junctures. The security considerations say these procedures have no direct impact on the security of the Internet. Appendix A gives sample reminder messages using a hypothetical FOO working group.
sections.plainLanguage: An early answer can go out of date, so people get asked again later. Nobody is made into a police officer; they just remind others.
